summary: Describes NAT-PMP, a protocol that automates creating NAT port mappings and lets a client learn the external IPv4 address of a NAT gateway. Apple products have implemented it since 2005. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Behind a NAT, a device cannot receive inbound connections unless someone configures the router by hand, which is unreasonably onerous for most residential users. NAT-PMP lets the device ask the router for the mapping itself, and tell the router how long it wants it to last.

questions: how to automatically create a port mapping on a nat
how does nat-pmp create a port mapping
subtitle: A protocol that lets a device behind a home router ask for an inbound port mapping, and learn its own public address.

tldr.problem: Behind a NAT, a device cannot receive inbound connections unless someone configures the router by hand, which is unreasonably onerous for most residential users.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends small UDP requests to its default gateway: one to ask what the gateway's external address is, and one to ask for a mapping of an internal port to an external port with a stated lifetime. The gateway answers with the result code, the external address and the port it actually allocated.
tldr.outcome: The mapping is soft state held by the client rather than the router, so if the router reboots and loses it, the client notices and recreates it automatically. The RFC also points to the successor protocol, PCP.

today: RFC 6886 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. The RFC itself names its successor: Port Control Protocol (PCP) in RFC 6887, which builds on NAT-PMP using the same UDP ports and a compatible packet format, and to which all existing NAT-PMP implementations are encouraged to migrate.

sections.title: Introduction: NAT, Mappings and the Problem
sections.content:
Network Address Translation is a method of sharing one public Internet address with a number of devices. This document focuses on devices formally classified as Network Address/Port Translators. A NAT has one or more external IP addresses, and a private network is set up behind it. Client devices on that private network are assigned private addresses and use the private address of the NAT device as their default gateway.

When a packet from a device behind the NAT is sent to the public Internet, the packet first passes through the NAT box. The NAT looks at the source port and address, and in some cases also keeps track of the destination port and address. It then creates a mapping from the internal address and internal port to an external address and external port, if a mapping does not already exist, replaces the internal address and port in the packet with the external entries from the mapping, and sends the packet on to the next gateway. When a packet from the Internet arrives on the NAT's external side, the NAT looks up the destination address and port in its list of mappings; if an entry is found it contains the internal address and port to which the packet should be sent, and the NAT rewrites the destination and forwards the packet. If the packet did not match any mapping, it will most likely be dropped, because the NAT does not know to which internal address the packet should be sent.

Mappings are usually created automatically as a result of observing outbound packets. There are a few exceptions: some NATs allow manually created permanent mappings that map an external port to a specific internal address and port, and some implement a default mapping where any inbound packet that does not match a more specific mapping is forwarded to a specified internal address. Both are usually set up manually through a configuration tool, and such manual configuration is unreasonably onerous for most residential NAT users.

Without these manually created inbound port mappings, clients behind the NAT would be unable to receive inbound connections, which represents a loss of connectivity compared with the original Internet architecture. NAT-PMP allows clients to operate more like a host directly connected to the unrestricted public Internet, by letting client hosts communicate with the NAT gateway to request the creation of inbound mappings on demand. Having created a mapping, the client can then record its external IPv4 address and external port in a public registry such as the Domain Name System, or otherwise make it accessible to peers that wish to communicate with it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that translates addresses keeps a table saying which internal address and port each external address and port belongs to. Outbound traffic creates those entries automatically. Inbound traffic only works if an entry exists, and until now that meant configuring the router by hand.

sections.title: The Protocol and Packet Format
sections.content:
The NAT Port Mapping Protocol runs over UDP. Every packet starts with an 8-bit version followed by an 8-bit operation code. All numeric quantities larger than a single byte, such as error values, Seconds Since Start of Epoch and mapping lifetime, are transmitted in the traditional IETF network byte order, most significant byte first. Non-numeric quantities larger than a single byte, such as the NAT gateway's external IP address, are transmitted in the natural byte order with no byte swapping.

This document specifies version 0 of the protocol. A gateway implementing this version that receives a request with any other version number must return result code 1, Unsupported Version, indicating the highest version number it does support in the version field of the response. Opcodes between 0 and 127 are client requests, and opcodes from 128 to 255 are the corresponding server responses. Responses always contain a 16-bit result code in network byte order, where zero indicates success. Responses also contain a 32-bit unsigned integer giving the number of seconds since the NAT gateway was rebooted or since its port mapping state was otherwise reset.

The protocol should only be used when the client determines that its primary IPv4 address is in one of the private IPv4 address ranges, which include 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. Clients always send their requests to their default gateway, as learned via DHCP or similar means. The protocol is designed for small home networks with a single logical link where the client's default gateway is also the NAT; for more complicated networks where the NAT is some device other than the client's default gateway, it is not appropriate.

To determine the external address, the client sends a request with version 0 and opcode 0 to port 5351 of the configured gateway address. A compatible gateway must reply with the same version, an opcode of 128 plus the request's opcode, a 16-bit result code, the 32-bit Seconds Since Start of Epoch value, and the 32-bit external IPv4 address. If the result code is non-zero, the external address field is undefined and must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception. The gateway must fill in the Seconds Since Start of Epoch field with the time elapsed since its port mapping table was initialized on startup, or reset for any other reason.

The gateway also announces address changes. Upon boot, acquisition of an external IPv4 address, a subsequent change of that address, a reboot, or any other event that may indicate possible loss or change of NAT mapping state, the gateway must send a gratuitous response to the link-local multicast address 224.0.0.1 on port 5350, to notify clients of the external address and the Seconds Since Start of Epoch. To accommodate packet loss, the gateway should multicast 10 address notifications, with the interval between the first two at 250 ms and the interval between each subsequent one doubling. The Seconds Since Start of Epoch field in each transmission must be updated to reflect the passage of time, so as not to trigger unnecessary additional mapping renewals.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is tiny and starts with a version byte and an opcode byte. A request asks for something; the reply adds a result code and tells the client how long the gateway has been up. The gateway also announces its public address by multicast, so a client learns about a change without having to ask.

sections.title: Requesting, Renewing and Destroying a Mapping
sections.content:
To create a mapping, the client sends a UDP packet to port 5351 of the gateway's internal IP address with the version, an opcode of 1 for Map UDP or 2 for Map TCP, a Reserved field that must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception, the Internal Port the client is listening on, a Suggested External Port, and the requested mapping lifetime in seconds.

If the client would prefer a high-numbered anonymous external port, it sets the Suggested External Port to zero, which asks the gateway to allocate a port of its choosing. If it would prefer the external port to match the internal port, it sets the field to the desired value. The gateway is not obliged to assign the suggested port, and may choose not to, either for policy reasons or because that port is already assigned to another client. The field exists for failure recovery: most low-cost home gateways do not record temporary port mappings in persistent storage, so if the gateway crashes or reboots, all the mappings are lost. A renewal packet is formatted identically to an initial request, except that the client sets the Suggested External Port to the port the gateway actually assigned, rather than the port the client originally wanted, which improves the stability of external ports across gateway restarts. The RECOMMENDED Port Mapping Lifetime is 7200 seconds, two hours.

The gateway replies with the version, an opcode of 128 plus the request's opcode, the result code, the Seconds Since Start of Epoch, the internal port, the mapped external port, and the lifetime in seconds. The gateway must be able to create TCP-only and UDP-only port mappings, and must not automatically create the other kind; if it silently created a pair for a client that asked for one, it could expose that client to inbound traffic it did not ask for. It must, however, reserve the companion port so the same client can map it later. The source address of the request packet must be used for the internal address in the mapping, because the protocol is not intended to let one device create mappings for other devices. The gateway must not accept mapping requests destined to its own external IP address or received on its external interface. The gateway may reduce the lifetime from what the client asked for, but should not offer one longer than was requested.

The client should begin renewing the mapping halfway to expiry, like DHCP. The renewal packet looks exactly the same as a request packet, except that the Suggested External Port is set to what the gateway previously mapped rather than what the client originally suggested.

A mapping may be destroyed in several ways. If the client fails to renew it, the mapping must be automatically deleted when its lifetime expires. When the gateway is a combined DHCP server and NAT gateway, a client's DHCP lease expiring may cause the gateway to delete that client's mappings, so that a new client assigned the same IP address does not receive unexpected inbound traffic. A client may also send an explicit deletion request, which is a mapping request with the Requested Lifetime set to zero and the Suggested External Port set to zero. On success the gateway responds with result code 0, the internal port, an external port of 0 and a lifetime of 0. A gateway must respond to a request to destroy a mapping that does not exist as if the request were successful, because a lost acknowledgement leads the client to retransmit. If the client tries to delete a mapping that was manually assigned by an administrator, the gateway must respond with a Not Authorized error, result code 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says which local port it wants exposed and for how long. The gateway may pick a different external port, and tells the client which one it got. The client renews halfway through the lifetime, and can ask for the mapping to be removed by asking for a lifetime of zero.

sections.title: Result Codes and Retransmission
sections.content:
The result codes currently defined are 0 for Success, 1 for Unsupported Version, 2 for Not Authorized or Refused, for example when the gateway supports mapping but the user has turned the feature off, 3 for Network Failure, for example when the NAT box itself has not obtained a DHCP lease, 4 for Out of resources, meaning the NAT box cannot create any more mappings at this time, and 5 for Unsupported opcode.

Because NAT gateways are often low-cost devices with limited memory and CPU speed, clients should not issue multiple concurrent requests, and should instead queue them and issue them serially, one at a time, waiting for the gateway to respond before sending the next. A fast gateway may complete requests at a rate of hundreds per second, while a slow gateway that takes perhaps half a second to respond should be allowed to operate at that pace rather than be overloaded.

To determine the external IPv4 address or to request a port mapping, a client sends its request packet to port 5351 of its configured gateway address and waits 250 ms for a response. If no response arrives after 250 ms, the client retransmits and waits 500 ms, and should repeat the process with the interval between attempts doubling each time. If, after sending its ninth attempt and then waiting for 64 seconds, the client has still received no response, it should conclude that the gateway does not support the protocol and may log an error message. If the client instead receives an ICMP Port Unreachable for port 5351, it can skip the remaining retransmissions and conclude immediately.

The client may record this information to suppress further attempts, but should not retain it for too long. Any event that may indicate a potential change of gateway or of gateway configuration, such as a hardware link change indication, a change of gateway MAC address, acquisition of a new DHCP lease, or receipt of a NAT-PMP announcement packet, should cause the client to discard its previous information and send its next request normally.
sections.plainLanguage: Six result codes say what happened, from success to out of resources. A client that gets no answer retries with a doubling wait, giving up after nine tries, and an unreachable-port reply lets it give up at once instead.

sections.title: Soft State: Recovering After a Gateway Reboot
sections.content:
Every packet sent by the gateway includes a Seconds Since Start of Epoch field. If the gateway resets or loses the state of its port mapping table, because of a reboot, a power failure or any other reason, it must reset its epoch time and count from zero again. Whenever a client receives any packet from the gateway, whether unsolicited or in response to a request, the client computes its own conservative estimate of the expected value by taking the value in the last packet it received and adding 7/8, that is 87.5%, of the time elapsed according to the client's local clock since that packet was received. If the new value is less than that estimate by more than 2 seconds, the client concludes that the gateway has rebooted or otherwise lost its mapping state, and must immediately renew all its active port mapping leases.

The gateway may store mappings in persistent storage so that it remembers the mapping state across a power cycle, but maintaining that state is not essential for correct operation. When it powers on or clears its mapping state as the result of a configuration change, it must reset the epoch time and re-announce its IPv4 address. Reception of that packet, where time has apparently gone backwards, serves as a hint to clients that they should immediately send renewal packets instead of waiting for the scheduled time.

A renewal packet is formatted identically to an original mapping request. From the point of view of the client it is a renewal of an existing mapping, but from the point of view of the freshly rebooted gateway it appears as a new mapping request. The RFC calls this self-healing property of the protocol very important. The reliability of the Internet derives in large part from important state being held in the endpoints rather than in the network itself: power-cycling an Ethernet switch results only in a brief interruption, and established TCP connections through it are not broken. NAT gateways are the exception, because the port mapping state is required for the gateway to know where to forward inbound packets, and losing it breaks connectivity. By letting clients detect the loss and recreate the state on demand, the protocol turns hard state in the network into soft state that is recovered automatically when needed.

The RFC's illustration is a network security camera that uses the protocol to accept incoming connections. It may operate for weeks, months or years, and in that time the gateway could suffer a power failure, a firmware upgrade, or be replaced entirely. The question is not whether the gateway will lose its mappings but when. If the camera can detect that and recreate them, the disruptions are self-correcting and largely invisible; if not, every gateway reboot requires the user to reset every other device on the network. That is the difference between a protocol that keeps working over months or years and one that works in brief testing but continually fails in the real world.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway counts how long it has been up since it last lost its mapping table, and says so in every message. The client notices when that count has gone backwards, which means the gateway restarted, and immediately asks for its mappings again. The state lives in the client, so a router reboot is repaired without anyone noticing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only a client on the internal side of the NAT may create port mappings, and it may do so only on its own behalf. By using IP address spoofing, it is possible for one client to delete the port mappings of another client, and it is possible for one client to create port mappings on behalf of another client. In cases where this is a concern, it can be dealt with using IPsec.

The multicast announcements could be spoofed, facilitating a denial-of-service attack. This makes the protocol unsuitable for use on LANs with large numbers of hosts where one or more of the hosts may be untrustworthy. Another concern is that rogue software running on a local host could create port mappings for unsuspecting hosts, rendering them vulnerable to external attack, although it is not clear how realistic that threat model is, since rogue software on a local host could attack such hosts directly without this indirect technique, and the concern rests on the assumption that a NAT gateway and a firewall are the same thing, which they are not.

Some people view the property of NATs blocking inbound connections as a security benefit that this protocol undermines. The authors take a different view: in the days before NAT became prevalent, all hosts had unique public IP addresses and unhindered ability to communicate with any other host on the Internet. Using NAT breaks that unhindered connectivity, relegating hosts to second-class status. The purpose of a NAT gateway should be to allow several hosts to share a single address, not to simultaneously impede those hosts' ability to communicate freely. Security is most properly provided by end-to-end cryptographic security and by explicit firewall functionality, as appropriate, and blocking of certain connections should occur only as a result of explicit and intentional firewall policy, not as an accidental side effect of some other technology. However, since many users do expect their NAT gateways to function as a kind of firewall, any gateway implementing this protocol should have an administrative mechanism to disable it, thereby restoring the pre-protocol behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Because there is no authentication, a device on your own network can ask for a mapping in your name or delete yours. The protocol is not suitable for networks where the devices cannot be trusted. The RFC also makes the point that blocking inbound connections is a firewall job, not something a NAT should do by accident.

fields.name: Operation
fields.desc: 1 for Map UDP, 2 for Map TCP.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: Internal Port
fields.desc: The local port on which the client is listening.

fields.name: Suggested External Port
fields.desc: The port the client would like, or zero to ask the gateway to choose.

fields.name: Requested Lifetime
fields.desc: Requested port mapping lifetime in seconds. The recommended value is 7200 seconds.

items.label: Unsupported Version
items.desc: The gateway does not implement the version in the request.

items.label: Not Authorized or Refused
items.desc: For example, the gateway supports mapping but the user has turned the feature off.

items.label: Network Failure
items.desc: For example, the NAT box itself has not obtained a DHCP lease.

items.label: Out of resources
items.desc: The NAT box cannot create any more mappings at this time.

items.label: Unsupported opcode
items.desc: The gateway does not implement the requested operation.

viz.caption: RECOVERING THE MAPPINGS AFTER A GATEWAY REBOOT

messages.label: Announcement (epoch reset to zero)
messages.note: Sent to the link-local multicast address on port 5350 after a reboot or a reset of the mapping table.

messages.label: Renewal for every active mapping
messages.note: Sent at once because the epoch has gone backwards, rather than at the scheduled time.

messages.label: Response
messages.note: The gateway treats the renewal as an ordinary new mapping request and recreates the mapping.
